thread.title: Guided by the people, Smith Snowden finds his place at Michigan
thread.title_full: Guided by the people, Smith Snowden finds his place at Michigan

author: Grace Wright
title: Guided by the people, Smith Snowden finds his place at Michigan
text:
Trotting out into a Skyridge High School varsity game his freshman year, Smith Snowden looked a tad out of place. The cornerback wore a jersey that hung off his slim frame, immediately identifying him as an easy target.
Tactically, the opponent’s quarterback singled Snowden out on almost every play during the drive he was in for. Despite his stature, Snowden was impactful — on the last play of the drive, he stuck to his man and disrupted the quarterback’s throw. In an uncharacteristic display of on-field emotion, Snowden rocketed the ball into the air, fueled by pride and glee.
The move may have cost the Falcons a 15-yard penalty and benched Snowden for the remainder of the game, but for Snowden and his teammates, it was well worth it.
“He had the opportunity to make a play,” Dre Snowden, Smith’s older brother, told The Michigan Daily. “And even though he was young, undersized, whatever, maybe he looked a little goofy in his uniform, there was nothing that was going to stop him from making the play. Every opportunity that comes his way, he will seize and that just is a testament to the kind of player that he is now.”
Smith has always been a bit undersized for a cornerback. In a perfect world, he’d stand at 6-foot-1 or 6-foot-2, but Smith’s 5-foot-10 frame is more than enough for him to make an impact, even if he may have been overlooked by his competition in the past.
Others’ perceptions and expectations don’t faze Smith, because at the end of the day he’s confident in his identity beyond football. Smith isn’t defined by the game. Instead, it’s the people and places around it that make Smith who he is.
***
When now-Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham made the decision to take the job with the Wolverines, Smith, a then-junior at Utah, didn’t immediately follow suit. He had an incredibly positive experience with the Utes staff, but Smith wasn’t going to pass up the opportunity to explore his options.
So he took some visits.
“He really got the opportunity to see what he was made of,” Dre said of Smith’s experience in the transfer portal.
Smith wasn’t underrecruited in high school, he just didn’t get the same national attention he did years later. The three-time first-team All-State honoree had a slew of scholarship offers, but he didn’t get those blue-blood big-name schools. In the thick of his high school recruitment, the top five schools Smith considered were Utah, BYU, Colorado State, Northwestern and Tennessee. They’re prominent programs in their own right, but for Smith, who’d dreamed of Ohio State in hopes of following in the footsteps of one of his favorite cornerbacks, Denzel Ward, the lack of big-name programs not recruiting him could’ve been seen as a slight.
To be frank, though, collegiate recruiters have a profile for who they believe will have a successful football career — and, once again, due to his slight undersize, Smith didn’t fit the criteria.
“If he was two inches taller, he would have had every single offer in the country,” Jon Leham, Smith’s high school coach, told The Daily. “Because he had the rest of the package.”
After three years with the Utes in which he showcased his talent to the nation, Smith’s second time dealing with the recruiting world told a different story.
“The biggest difference between the high school recruitment and when he was in the transfer portal was the fact that everyone understood exactly what they were getting,” Dre said.
So while Smith had really positive relationships with the Utah coaching staff that was moving to Michigan. He knew that to explore all his options — maybe even to fulfill some of those high school recruiting dreams — and take the visits. Smith and his family had many meaningful conversations about his next steps, and ultimately the decision was clear. He needed to go where his people were.
“I think a lot of the jump from Utah to Michigan was not only getting the opportunity, showing what he can do,” Lehman said. “But also trusting the people that are involved in that process.”
Michigan not only had the pedigree to give Smith the best chance at pursuing a professional career, but he also had pre-established relationships that he felt would set him up for success.
***
Now-Wolverines cornerbacks coach Jernaro Gilford has known the Snowden family for decades. Gilford not only played with Smith’s dad, Will Snowden, at BYU, but was also his freshman year roommate and has been a family friend since. While Gilford didn’t coach Smith in an official sense until this season, the relationship still guided Smith’s career. And Gilford was already aware of Smith’s talent on the gridiron, dating all the way back to when he first saw him play 13 years ago.
Taking a trip back to Utah to visit Will, Gilford just happened to be in town for one of Smith’s Pop Warner football games. Will was one of the team’s coaches, so Gilford went to the game not only to support his friend, but to see Will’s son play. Gilford recalls it as the first time he knew Smith was a unique athlete at the ripe age of 8 years old.
Playing quarterback at the time, Smith was running all around the field and got leveled on a particularly intense hit. As any child would, Smith hit the ground and tears started flowing. After some stern encouragement from Will, Smith got back up. And on the very next play, he ran 70-some yards for a touchdown.
“He’s always been a guy who makes plays,” Gilford told The Daily. “He’s always been a guy that people look up to because of the way he carries himself. He still carries himself in a professional manner, which is a great thing. And just his background from mom, dad and family. He’s genuinely a good person.”
Gilford is now coaching a much more established and confident 21-year-old Smith, but the bones of that 8-year-old athlete are still in him. He’s a bounce-back, self-assured player who performs not only for himself, but for those around him.
***
Smith has continued throughout his career to craft the skills that once made him successful as a kid. He’s always had a savvy playmaking ability and explosive tendencies that make him a threat in the backfield. But building on those natural talents, Smith has become a technician.
Smith strives to always be in the right place at the right time, to take educated risks and be a threat, no matter where he is on the field. It was during his 2025 season with the Utes that Smith had the opportunity to piece all of those skills together to perform. Smith’s mentality is reflective of his playstyle, as he relishes the opportunity to play man coverage. With all the attention on just him and the receiver, Smith is ready to take on the challenge and is emboldened by the spotlight.
“I do take pride when it comes to man,” Smith told The Daily. “It’s me versus you. It makes it simple, me versus you, let’s go.”
When Utah took on Arizona State last year, Smith had a breakout performance. Matched up against Sun Devils wide receiver Jordan Tyson — the future No. 8 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft — Smith knew he was considered the underdog. Instead of balking at the challenge, though, it only excited Smith more. Smith didn’t give Tyson any extra room to work with, breaking up two passes and holding Tyson to his second-fewest receiving yards all season.
“His football IQ and intelligence of the game,” Gilford said of what makes Smith stand out. “Knowing things that are coming before they come. Very, very sticky as far as coverage goes, always in a good position. Takes educated guesses about what’s coming so he can be in the right position to make plays and just being a student of the game.”
For Smith, his time at Utah was a chance to show the college football stage what he, and those close to him, knew all along. Smith Snowden is not only a natural talent but a student of the game, and if you happen to be the opposing receiver, you better hope you aren’t his assignment.
***
Football was always in the cards for Smith. The Snowdens are a family chock-full of talented athletes, and many of them made their name on the gridiron. Smith’s grandfather, dad, uncle and two older brothers all played collegiate football before Smith. So it just made sense for him to follow in those footsteps.
“I kind of knew I was always gonna play football,” Smith said. “It was one of my first loves.”
Even with all of the football influence around him, Smith isn’t defined by the game. Sure, he’s a talented athlete and certainly competitive when it comes to game days. But football isn’t his entire world. Instead, it’s all the things around the game that give Smith the excitement for the sport.
It’s his brother Dre, who’s been training Smith since he was a kid. It’s his dad, who walked him through both recruitment processes but trusted him to make the best decision for himself. It’s Gilford, who has been in Smith’s circle for as long as he can remember, and who he now has a chance to work with every day.
Smith doesn’t describe himself as uber competitive. His family and friends use words like “loyal” and “kind” to describe him before jumping to any of his athletic prowess. Beyond the final score or the game itself, Smith is sure to enjoy the process along the way.
“Win, lose or anything else, his identity is firm and established and he’s going to be fine,” Lehman said.
It’s this reason that he took visits in the transfer portal, that he chose Utah over his dad’s alma mater, that he studies film and wants to be the most technical athlete on the field. For Smith, each individual moment and person is just as important as the game itself.
***
Smith Snowden is a technician. He is a student of the game who is always striving to get better. But despite being a talented cornerback who’s worked his way up through the ranks of collegiate football, being a football player isn’t Smith’s calling card.
“Everything’s not wrapped up in how he does on the football field,” Lehman said. “He’s got a sense of purpose that’s bigger than that, and so I don’t think that his identity is all ‘I am a football player.’ I think his identity is a lot bigger than that.”
Football is simply one facet of many that make Smith up. Playing the game isn’t Smith’s end-all be-all, but he sure as hell will enjoy the journey that it gives him.
